youtube.baslik: Vestibular Rehab for Children and Older Adults | Lesson 261 | AIHEAR Audiology Academy
youtube.aciklama:
How is vestibular rehabilitation adapted for children and older adults? In this lesson we cover vestibular loss and motor delay in children with hearing loss, play-based exercise, safe progression in older adults, and how rehabilitation fits into fall prevention programs.

AIHEAR Audiology Academy makes short, clear lessons for audiology students and professionals.

Sources: Herdman and Clendaniel, Vestibular Rehabilitation; Hall et al., Vestibular Rehabilitation for Peripheral Vestibular Hypofunction: An Updated Clinical Practice Guideline, J Neurol Phys Ther (2022); Inoue et al., Effect of vestibular dysfunction on the development of gross motor function in children with profound hearing loss, Audiol Neurotol (2013); Rine et al., Improvement of motor development and postural control following intervention in children with sensorineural hearing loss and vestibular impairment, Int J Pediatr Otorhinolaryngol (2004); Sherrington et al., Exercise for preventing falls in older people living in the community, Cochrane Database Syst Rev (2019).

This video is for educational purposes and does not replace diagnosis or treatment.

sahneler.baslik: *Vestibular* rehab for children and older adults
sahneler.alt: Play-based exercise, safe progression, fall prevention
cumleler: Hello, and welcome to the AIHEAR Audiology Academy.
In this lesson we will learn how vestibular rehabilitation is adapted at both ends of life, in children and in older adults.
We will cover motor development and play-based exercise in children, and safety and fall prevention in older adults.
Adaptation, habituation and sensory substitution, which we saw in earlier lessons, are the basic tools of rehabilitation at any age.
What changes is who these tools are applied to, and how.
In children the balance system is still developing; vestibular loss can also affect gaining motor skills such as walking.
In older adults, vision, body sense and muscle strength have also weakened with age; the program is built around these limits.
Studies show that age alone is not a barrier to rehabilitation; older adults benefit too.

cumleler.yazi: The 2022 American Physical Therapy Association guideline focuses on adults; in children the evidence rests on fewer studies.
cumleler.ses: The twenty twenty two American Physical Therapy Association guideline focuses on adults; in children the evidence rests on fewer studies.

sahneler.baslik: Vestibular loss in children: *common* and silent

maddeler.metin: Causes: CMV, meningitis, inner ear anomaly

cumleler: Vestibular dysfunction is more common than expected in children with sensorineural hearing loss.
According to studies, about 20 to 70 percent of these children have some degree of loss in the vestibular organs.
Congenital cytomegalovirus, or CMV infection, bacterial meningitis and inner ear anomalies are among the main causes.
In Usher syndrome type 1, profound hearing loss comes with congenital bilateral vestibular loss.
A child with congenital loss does not know the feeling of spinning, so often does not complain of dizziness.
Families more often notice motor signs such as clumsiness, frequent falls, late sitting or late walking.
Cochlear implant surgery can also reduce vestibular function in some children, so balance testing before implantation matters.

notlar.metin: Head control and walking may be delayed

cumleler: A typically developing baby gains head control at about 3 to 4 months and sits without support at about 6 months.
Independent walking starts around age 1 in most children; walking up to 18 months is still within the usual range.
In a study of 89 children with profound hearing loss, those with abnormal vestibular tests gained head control later.
This motor delay was also seen in walking; it was most marked in children with all three tests abnormal.
The red dots in the diagram are an example of this delay; real ages vary from child to child.
Most children eventually walk, but later they may struggle with skills such as standing on one leg and riding a bicycle.
The process starts with the motor milestones the family reports: head control, sitting, walking and how often the child falls.
Vestibular function is assessed with tests adapted to the child's age; we saw this battery in the lesson on dizziness in children.
Gross motor skills are assessed separately by a pediatric physical therapist with standard motor tests.
Goals are chosen with the family from daily life; for example, climbing the playground ladder without help.
Once the program starts, motor tests and family observations are repeated at set intervals.

ogeler.metin: Look at a sticker, shake head

cumleler: Young children find repetitive exercise boring, so for them exercise is set up as play-based therapy.
Gaze stabilization can become a game of looking at a sticker on the wall while shaking the head yes and no.
Walking on a line on the floor, standing on a mat and carrying a beanbag on the head can be used for balance.
Obstacle courses with climbing, bending and jumping build gross motor skills and confidence together.
Freeze games when the music stops and catching a ball train balance reactions and eye hand coordination.
Small controlled studies show the benefit of exercise programs that target motor development and balance in children.

maddeler.metin: Sense of success: easy to hard
The family becomes the _coach_ at home

cumleler: A child's attention span is short; exercises are split into chunks of a few minutes with breaks in between.
Tasks start at a level the child can achieve; they get harder as the child succeeds, and success is rewarded with praise.
Most repetition happens at home; the family learns to build exercises into daily routines such as bath time, dressing and the park.
Balance games are played on a soft surface under close adult supervision.
In a child with motion sensitivity, habituation exercises start at a very low dose; symptoms should settle quickly.
The hearing aid or implant should be on during exercise; sounds are also an important cue for orientation.

maddeler.metin: Helmet on bikes, beware slippery floors
Inform teachers and physical education staff

cumleler: A child with bilateral vestibular loss can become disoriented when vision and foot sensation are reduced.
Underwater or in murky water, telling up from down can be hard; swimming should only be done with close supervision.
Since balance can worsen markedly in the dark, a night light and a well-lit hallway are simple but effective measures.
Protective gear is used for activities such as cycling and skating; the aim is not to restrict the child but to let them join in safely.
Informing the classroom teacher and the physical education teacher prevents the child from being misunderstood at school.

notlar.metin: Benefit does not disappear with age

cumleler: We saw fall risk in older adults in an earlier lesson; now let us look at how rehabilitation is adapted for them.
With age, central compensation, meaning the brain making up for the loss, may slow down; progress may take longer.
Even so, studies show that older adults also gain meaningful benefit from vestibular rehabilitation.
The main difference lies in coexisting problems: vision, joints, muscle strength, cognition and fear of falling shape the program.
So in older adults the goal is not only less dizziness, but walking safely and doing daily tasks independently.
Before exercise, ask about a drop in blood pressure on standing, or orthostatic hypotension; if present, share it with the physician.
If foot sensation is reduced, for example by diabetes, the load on vision and the vestibular system for balance increases.
Multifocal lenses can blur the view of the floor while walking; this affects the choice of exercises.
Vestibular suppressants and sedating medications can slow compensation; decisions on medication belong to the physician.
Cognition and hearing determine whether instructions are understood; a person with hearing loss also gets them in writing.
Rugs, lighting and stairs at home determine where and how the home exercises will be done.

adimlar.metin: At a counter, in a corner
In a hallway, turning the head

cumleler: In older adults, gaze stabilization exercises often start in a seated position.
Standing exercises are first done at a kitchen counter or in the corner of a room, with support within reach.
Once the person can stand safely, support is reduced and the feet are brought closer together.
Then come tasks such as turning the head left and right while walking; a long hallway is a good place to start.
In the final stage, dual tasks are added, such as walking outdoors, on uneven ground or while talking.

maddeler.metin: Fear of falling is also targeted

cumleler.yazi: A 2019 Cochrane review of exercise programs for older adults living in the community gave an important result.
cumleler.ses: A twenty nineteen Cochrane review of exercise programs for older adults living in the community gave an important result.

cumleler: Exercise cut the number of falls by about a quarter; the strongest evidence is for balance and functional exercises.
Programs that combine balance exercise with muscle strengthening were also found effective.
The Otago program, developed in New Zealand, is a good example of strength and balance exercises done at home.
Fear of falling can leave a person inactive; rehabilitation also aims to rebuild confidence step by step.
When vestibular exercises are built into fall prevention programs, the older adult follows a single, consistent plan.

sahneler.baslik: Children and older adults: *side by side*
cumleler: In children the aim is to support motor development; in older adults it is a safe and independent daily life.
In children exercise is built into play and daily routines; in older adults it progresses gradually from supported to unsupported.
In both groups the main risk is falling; disorientation stands out in children, fractures and inactivity in older adults.
The family and school are partners in the program for children; caregivers and the health team for older adults.
At both ends of life the program is written for the individual and readjusted with regular measurements.

sahneler.metin: Use pictures and large print on the home exercise sheet. Note where older adults hold on and name the game for children; practice once together.
cumleler: A clinical tip: when giving the home exercise program in writing, use pictures and large letters.
For an older adult, write next to each exercise where to hold on; for example, in front of the kitchen counter.
For a child, give each exercise a game name; names like the sticker game help the family remember at home.
Before handing over the program, have the person or family do it once in front of you; a wrong exercise is corrected right away.

maddeler.metin: Vestibular loss in children: common, silent

cumleler: Vestibular loss is common in children with hearing loss and often shows up as motor delay rather than complaints.
In children, exercises are built into play and daily routines; the family is the program's coach at home.
In older adults the program is built around coexisting problems, moving from seated to supported standing, then walking.
Balance and strength exercises reduce falls in older adults; vestibular exercises are built into these programs.

sahneler.soru: How do standing exercises start in older adults?
sahneler.aciklama: Standing exercises start _with support nearby_, then support is reduced.

cumleler.yazi: Test yourself: how are standing balance exercises usually started in an older adult?

cumleler: The correct answer is B: with support to hold on to nearby, for example in front of a counter.
Support is reduced as the person stands safely; uneven ground and dual tasks are later stages.
